paragraphs.heading: What mitigation means
paragraphs.text: Climate change mitigation, also called decarbonisation, is action to limit greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, the gases that cause climate change. It includes saving energy and swapping fossil fuels for clean energy sources. Secondary strategies include changes to how land is used and removing carbon dioxide (CO₂) from the atmosphere.

paragraphs.heading: Where the emissions come from
paragraphs.text: Human activities emit greenhouse gases, and these emissions strengthen the greenhouse effect, which contributes to climate change. Most of the emissions are carbon dioxide released by burning the fossil fuels coal, oil and natural gas. In 2016, 73.2% of greenhouse gas emissions came from energy used for electricity, heat and transport. Agriculture, forestry and land use accounted for 18.4%, direct industrial processes for 5.2% and waste for 3.2%. Coal-fired power stations are the largest single source, with 20% of greenhouse gas emissions.

paragraphs.heading: The gap between goals and policy
paragraphs.text: Assessments from 2022 stress that, to limit warming to 1.5 °C, global greenhouse gas emissions must peak before 2025 and fall by about 43% by 2030. The policies adopted so far are insufficient. Under them, the world would still warm by about 2.7 °C by 2100. That is significantly above the goal of the 2015 Paris Agreement, which is to limit global warming to below 2 °C.

paragraphs.heading: Clean electricity
paragraphs.text: Of the renewable energy options, solar energy and wind power are the cheapest way to replace fossil fuels. Sunshine and wind are variable, though, and this can require upgrades to the electrical grid, such as moving electricity over long distances to group a range of power sources. Storing energy can also smooth out power output, and demand management can limit how much power is used when generation is low. Electricity generated cleanly can usually take the place of fossil fuels for powering transport, heating buildings and running industrial processes.

paragraphs.heading: The harder cases
paragraphs.text: Air travel and cement production are examples of processes that are harder to decarbonise. Carbon capture and storage (CCS) can be an option for reducing net emissions in these circumstances. Fossil fuel power plants fitted with CCS technology, however, are currently a high-cost mitigation strategy.

paragraphs.heading: Land, food and methane
paragraphs.text: Human changes to land use, such as agriculture and deforestation, cause about a quarter of climate change. They affect how much CO₂ plant matter absorbs and how much organic matter decays or burns and releases CO₂. Methane is a short-lived greenhouse gas that comes from livestock, from decaying organic matter and from fossil fuel extraction. Emissions from agriculture can be cut by reducing food waste, by switching to a more plant-based diet and by improving farming processes.

paragraphs.heading: Policies that push change
paragraphs.text: Various policies can encourage mitigation. Carbon pricing systems have been set up that put a tax on CO₂ emissions, or that cap total emissions and let emission credits be traded. Subsidies for fossil fuels can be dropped in favour of subsidies for clean energy, and incentives can be offered for installing energy efficiency measures or for switching to electric power. Another issue is overcoming environmental objections when new clean energy sources are built and the grid is modified.
